claims.text: The initial material is an as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type alloy produced as melt-spun microribbons.
The as-deposited microribbons have an ordered, single-phase hexagonal structure.
The as-deposited microribbons have high residual stress.
The as-deposited microribbons have a high density of defects.
Annealing at 500–700 °C for 1–5 hours is a phase-safe processing window for this alloy.
Moderate post-deposition annealing relieves internal stress in the microribbons.
Moderate post-deposition annealing reduces dislocation and vacancy density in the microribbons.
Heat treatment can tune atomic short-range ordering in the alloy.
Ordered and disordered regions act as local energy barriers during the magnetostructural transition.
Reducing lattice-defect density through annealing produces more uniform atomic ordering.
Stress relief, defect reduction, and more uniform ordering smooth the energy barriers for the phase transformation.
Smoothing the transformation barriers broadens the initially sharp magnetostructural transition.
Smoothing the transformation barriers reduces hysteresis during low-applied-field cycling.
Annealed samples retain a significant magnetocaloric entropy change despite transition broadening.
Within the proposed safe window, longer or higher-temperature anneals further reduce hysteresis relative to the as-deposited state.
The as-deposited microribbons exhibit a large, sharp, and hysteretic magnetostructural transition.
The sharp magnetostructural transition limits heat-exchange rates.
The as-deposited state has high energy barriers for the phase transformation.
Annealing beyond the phase-stability window can produce unwanted secondary phases.
A substantial ordering change and defect-density reduction without transition broadening or hysteresis reduction would falsify the proposed stress/defect-governed mechanism.
